title: A fridge that supports the week you actually have
intro: Weekly meal prep in Dubai should make the days ahead easier to manage, not leave you with a rigid menu you stop enjoying. A chef can prepare selected meals in your kitchen around your preferences, appetite and available storage. The useful starting point is your diary: which lunches and dinners will you eat at home, and which meals need to be quick to finish? From there, the menu can balance familiar favourites, variety and practical portions. This guide helps you turn a weekly visit into food you genuinely look forward to using.

sections.title: Build a meal plan around real eating occasions
paragraphs: Count the meals you want covered rather than requesting an arbitrary number of dishes. Two adults who eat lunch at the office have a different brief from a family with children at home after school. Include the days when you usually order in or arrive home late, because those may be the most valuable meals to prepare.

Let us know whether you prefer complete portions or separate components you can combine. Both can work, but the chef needs to know before planning quantities and containers. The written scope confirms the visit, grocery arrangements and any additional requests.

sections.title: Decide what should be cooked now and finished later
paragraphs: Meal preparation starts with when you expect to eat each dish. Some food is best cooked and served during the visit; other meals can be prepared for later with appropriate storage and finishing instructions. Tell the chef which portions are for the next meal and which are intended for another day so the plan can reflect that difference.

Rather than asking for as many containers as possible, prioritise the meals that will genuinely be used. A smaller selection of well-planned lunches and dinners can be more valuable than a crowded fridge of similar dishes. Consider whether you want complete meals or separate proteins, vegetables and sides that you can combine yourself.

Storage capacity is part of the brief. Agree suitable containers, labelling and any dish-specific handling instructions with the chef. There is no single storage period that suits every recipe and household situation. If you are uncertain about a prepared item, ask before serving it rather than relying on a general assumption.

sections.title: Use portion feedback to improve the next visit
paragraphs: Guest count is only the beginning of portion planning. Appetite, meal timing and the number of dishes all affect how much food is useful. Tell us whether lunch is usually light, dinner is the main meal or family members have very different appetites. For a recurring arrangement, actual feedback is more useful than guessing a perfect quantity at the outset.

After a few meals, note what was finished, what remained and whether anyone wanted a larger serving. Distinguish between useful leftovers and food that simply went uneaten. That information can help the chef adjust quantities and choose dishes that fit the household more closely on the next visit.

If visitors are joining, update the headcount before shopping and preparation are finalised. Extra portions can affect ingredients, service time and the equipment required. Clear communication gives the chef room to plan properly and helps keep the experience generous without treating unnecessary food waste as a sign of good hospitality.

link.label: Keep your household plan up to date

sections.title: Agree how ingredients reach your kitchen
paragraphs: There are two practical starting points for groceries: have the agreed ingredients ready before the visit, or discuss shopping as part of the service. Either way, the menu needs a clear list. Quantities, preferred brands and acceptable alternatives help avoid delays when an ingredient is unavailable or a household staple has run out.

Keep the service fee and grocery spending easy to understand. Your written proposal should explain who shops, whether shopping time is included in the booked hours and how ingredient costs are handled. If you want a premium cut, specialist imported item or a particular organic product, include that in the brief so it can be priced and sourced appropriately.

It also helps to identify what is already in the kitchen. A quick check of oils, seasonings, rice and other staples can reduce duplicate purchases. For ongoing cooking, agree how the chef should flag low stock and ask before making substitutions that materially change the meal or its cost.

sections.title: Keep the menu interesting without making it complicated
paragraphs: A good menu has both familiarity and variety. Repeating a handful of favourite ingredients can make shopping more efficient, but repeating the same dish every visit can quickly feel limiting. Discuss a balance of reliable favourites and occasional new ideas, using different cooking methods, vegetables and accompaniments to keep meals appealing.

For example, a household that enjoys chicken might alternate a lemon and herb roast, gently spiced skewers and a lighter dish with grains and vegetables. The point is not to prescribe a fixed menu. It is to show how one preference can lead to several distinct meals that suit the available equipment and preparation time.

Ask for menus you can review easily. Clear dish descriptions are more useful than elaborate names that hide unfamiliar ingredients. If a meal is intended for reheating, check that the proposed texture and presentation will still work later. The best weekly menu is one you understand, enjoy and can use comfortably.

sections.title: Build one menu around different family appetites
paragraphs: Family cooking works best when the meal feels connected, even if every plate is a little different. A roast, grilled protein or vegetable dish can become the centre of the table, with sauces and sides served separately. This gives people some choice without turning dinner into several unrelated menus that compete for kitchen time.

Tell us about children's usual mealtimes, preferred textures and portion sizes. Some families want familiar dishes throughout the week; others would like gentle introductions to new flavours. Both can be discussed without promising that a particular meal will change anyone's eating habits. For younger children, parents should confirm age-appropriate requirements and any professional advice that needs to be followed.

Think beyond the main meal. You may want a portion set aside for someone arriving late, a lunchbox component or a simple breakfast preparation. These requests should be included in the brief so the chef can plan quantities and priorities rather than fitting extra tasks into an already full visit.

sections.title: End the visit with a clear kitchen handover
paragraphs: Before the chef leaves, make sure you understand what has been prepared and how it is intended to be used. Identify the meal for immediate service, the portions prepared for later and any dish that still needs a finishing step. Written labels or agreed notes can be useful when another family member will be serving the food.

Check the practical points that matter to your home: where containers have been placed, which serving items are in use and whether ingredients remain for the next visit. The agreed cleanup scope should also be clear, including the work surfaces and equipment used during cooking. A good handover reduces the need to search for information after the service has ended.

For a recurring plan, note anything that needs replenishing or changing before the next appointment. For a one-off dinner, confirm how any hired items or additional equipment will be collected. The final few minutes should leave you with a usable kitchen and a clear understanding of the food and arrangements.

cta.title: Let’s shape the details around you.
cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
